5	We test on synthetic ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K \in \{2, 4\}$, controlled $\Delta\tau$ and $\Delta\pi$, 100 Monte Carlo (MC) runs) and semi-synthetic data-generating processes (DGPs) spanning four NLP tasks: sentiment analysis (TweetEval~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, $K{=}4$), hate speech detection (CivilComments, $K{=}4$), stance detection ($K{=}5$; Appendix~\ref{app:stance}), and topic classification (AG News, $K{=}4$; Appendix~\ref{app:agnews}), with full specifications in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.

988	Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is derived under symmetric misclassification (A2); real LLM confusion matrices are asymmetric (FPR $\neq$ FNR).
989	We verify that the generalized identity $\mathrm{bias}(z,s) = \Delta\tau \cdot [B_s]_{z,1}$ (Remark~\ref{rem:asymmetric}) holds under real annotation error structures by running semi-synthetic simulations ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K{=}4$, $\Delta\tau{=}0.30$, 100 MC runs) with confusion matrices drawn from 11 LLM--dataset combinations: eight models on TweetEval (GPT-4-turbo, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5-turbo, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) and three on Civil Comments (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5-turbo).

992	The aggregate $R^2 = 0.975$; 10 of 11 combinations achieve $R^2 \geq 0.92$.

994	$R^2$ correlates strongly with $\max|[B_s]_{z,1}|$: models with more heterogeneous per-subgroup error rates produce larger bias signals that are easier to verify empirically.

When these noisy labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, the standard remedy, estimating a single confusion matrix and applying its inverse uniformly, is widely trusted to remove bias. We prove it can do the opposite. We derive an exact bias identity showing that global correction introduces a subgroup-level bias proportional to the interaction of error-rate deviation and effect heterogeneity, a product structure invisible to any pooled analysis. This identity reveals that correction reverses estimated causal effect signs in 14.9% of configurations and amplifies bias across all eight real LLMs tested. A diagnostic corollary flags harmful correction from error rates alone, without estimating treatment effects. Guided by the identity, we propose EC-HTE, a per-subgroup correction via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation that reduces bias by 7.4x under extreme heterogeneity, with clear operating conditions (delta_pi > 0.15, n_expert >= 250, K <= 4) and validated across 11 LLM-dataset combinations spanning four NLP tasks.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Standard confusion-matrix correction can reverse causal conclusions when misclassification rates vary across subgroups.
We derived an exact bias identity ($R^2 \geq 0.97$) that yields a diagnostic for flagging harmful correction and prescribes per-subgroup correction when $\Delta\pi > 0.15$ and $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$, validated across 11 LLM--dataset combinations spanning eight LLMs and four NLP tasks.

When these conditions are not met, global correction remains appropriate; the diagnostic explicitly guards against inappropriate application.
The framework is task-agnostic and composes with prediction-powered inference~\cite{sui2026ppci}.

A key implication is that aggregate annotation accuracy, the metric most commonly reported in LLM annotation studies, is insufficient for downstream causal validity.
Two annotators with identical overall accuracy can produce qualitatively different causal conclusions if their error distributions across subgroups differ, as our CivilComments case study demonstrates (3.2$\times$ effect-size gap between identity subgroups masked by global correction).
The bias identity formalizes this insight: the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ product structure shows that harm concentrates precisely where it is hardest to detect, in subgroups whose low error rates make them appear least problematic.

More broadly, as LLM annotation becomes standard practice in computational social science, the gap between average accuracy and subgroup-level reliability will grow with the diversity of populations studied.
Our bias identity provides a principled lens for auditing any pipeline that feeds machine-generated labels into downstream causal analysis; we release an open-source implementation to facilitate adoption.
Future directions include continuous covariates, larger $K$, and joint covariate--outcome correction.
